glance: Anthropic's first day on Nasdaq ended 17% above its IPO price after a much higher start. In Europe, electric car sales passed 2.3 million for the year while Volkswagen and IG Metall head for a hard pay fight and Volvo Cars' cutbacks reach its suppliers. Sweden's Algoryx gets Wallenberg backing for physics simulation, and Siemens and Deutsche Telekom push AI further into factory software and robot training.
brief: This is Vertical News for Friday the twentieth of November. Anthropic's shares began trading on Nasdaq yesterday. The first trade came just before noon at about one hundred and eleven dollars, thirty-four percent above the eighty-three dollar offer price, and the stock closed at about ninety-seven dollars, seventeen percent higher. The listing raised around eighty-one billion dollars. In Europe, electric car sales passed two point three million for the year, after October registrations jumped sixty-one percent and battery cars took about a third of the market. That comes as Parliament prepares to vote on softening the 2035 CO2 target. Volkswagen wants a two-year pay freeze and longer hours without extra pay, while IG Metall has called the first full-day strikes in eight years at BMW, Audi, Porsche and suppliers. In Sweden, seat maker Adient may cut about a hundred jobs in Gothenburg after Volvo Cars reduced output, even as the new EX60 won a UK car of the year award. BMW has started building the electric iX5 in South Carolina, using cylindrical cells from AESC, which has now shipped ten million of them. Ford has shipped its first American-made LFP cells, and Sany plans to undercut European truck makers by twenty percent. OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Accounting. Swedish simulation firm Algoryx gained Wallenberg Investments as an owner. Siemens ended forced project upgrades in its automation software, and Deutsche Telekom will train robot skills in simulation. Analysts weighed Schaeffler's China exposure and SKF's Vertevo spin-off. Finally, two new papers improve bearing fault diagnosis using motor current and changing operating conditions.

stories.headline: Anthropic's shares start trading 34% above the IPO price and close 17% higher
stories.why: The biggest AI listing yet sets a public price on a frontier lab whose models many product and engineering teams build on.
body: Anthropic's Class A shares, ticker ANT, began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday. The stock did not trade at the 9:30 open; after Nasdaq's opening auction for new listings, the first trade came at 11:48 a.m. Eastern at 111.50 dollars, about 34% above the 83-dollar IPO price set the evening before. It peaked near 115 dollars within minutes, fell to about 92.70 dollars in the early afternoon and closed at 97.17 dollars, according to Stock Titan's live coverage.

The IPO sold 980 million shares at 83 dollars, raising about 81.3 billion dollars before fees, most of it new money for Anthropic. The price had already been set above the marketed range of 70 to 78 dollars. Stock Titan values the company at about 1.1 trillion dollars on all share classes at the IPO price; other outlets quote higher, fully diluted figures, so headline valuations vary by method.

For teams that rely on Claude, a public Anthropic means quarterly reporting, more scrutiny of pricing and capacity, and pressure to show revenue growth. Expect the closing price, rather than the first trade, to anchor coverage in the coming days.

stories.headline: Europe's electric car sales pass 2.3 million for the year as October jumps 61%
stories.why: Demand is rising just as the EU decides how far to soften the 2035 CO2 target, which shapes OEM and supplier product plans.
body: New figures for 18 European markets show 295,252 electric cars registered in October, up 61% on a year earlier. That takes the year-to-date total to 2,334,832, up 41%. Battery electric cars made up 32.1% of new registrations in October, against about 20% a year before, and 25.3% on average so far this year.

France and Germany together accounted for more than half of October's electric registrations. Growth was fastest in smaller markets such as Slovenia, Romania and Czechia, while Sweden rose 10%. Italy was the only market where October's share was below its average for the year. The trade group E-Mobility Europe called it a market that is accelerating, not retreating.

The numbers land in the middle of the CO2 debate. On 4 November the European Parliament's environment committee voted 48 to 30 for an 87.5% cut in new-car CO2 by 2035, with credits that could take it to 95%. The full Parliament still has to vote, and the current 100% target stands until the law changes. For engineering teams, stronger demand argues against slowing EV programmes even if the target is relaxed.

stories.headline: Volkswagen asks for a two-year pay freeze as IG Metall calls full-day strikes at BMW, Audi and Porsche
stories.why: Labour costs and strike risk are now central to German automotive planning, from OEM plants to the supplier base.
body: Volkswagen set out its demands on Thursday for talks on its in-house wage agreement, which covers about 120,000 workers. It wants a two-year pay freeze, an end to a bonus that staff can take as cash or time off, and a reopening of the 35-hour week, with longer hours but no extra pay. IG Metall is asking for 5%. Talks begin on 24 November in Emden, one of four plants that could close from the early 2030s, and workers have threatened strikes from January.

In the wider metal and electrical industry round, which covers 3.7 million workers, IG Metall called 24-hour warning strikes from Friday, the first full-day strikes in eight years. BMW, Audi, Porsche and suppliers are affected. Employers have offered a one-off payment in July 2027 and a permanent 1.3% rise from summer 2028; the union wants 5% plus job security.
For suppliers and engineering service firms, the two disputes add up to a risk of production gaps in early 2027 and continued pressure to move work out of Germany.

stories.headline: Volvo Cars' production cuts hit seat maker Adient, with about 100 layoffs in Gothenburg
stories.why: The slowdown at Torslanda is now reaching West Sweden's supplier base, even as the new EX60 collects awards.
body: Seat supplier Adient told staff in Gothenburg on Thursday that about 100 jobs are at risk, after Volvo Cars sharply cut its orders. Output at Torslanda, mainly of the XC60 and XC90, has fallen. Volvo's October sales were down 25% to 45,264 cars, and it reported an operating loss of 5.6 billion kronor for the third quarter. In October it announced 5 billion kronor in further savings and about 2,500 job cuts, roughly 2,000 of them in Sweden.

The EX60, built on the new SPA3 platform, has more than 50,000 European orders but is ramping up more slowly than planned. The same day it was named Carwow Car of the Year 2027 in the UK, with a claimed range of up to 503 miles and 10–80% charging in 19 minutes in its top version.
For engineers at Swedish suppliers and consultancies, the signal is that volume relief depends on how fast the EX60 ramp goes, not on the older models.

stories.headline: BMW starts building the iX5 in South Carolina as AESC passes 10 million 46120 cells
stories.why: BMW's first US-built EV shows how large-format cylindrical cells are moving into series cars, and how cautious volume plans have become.
body: BMW has started series production of the electric iX5 at Spartanburg, its first EV built in the United States, at about 70 cars a day according to US reports. Suppliers have been told to plan for 60,000 units of capacity in 2027, down from an earlier 100,000. The car uses a 141 kWh battery assembled in nearby Woodruff. The electric iX7 will follow at the same plant.

Cell maker Envision AESC said it has delivered more than 10 million 46120 cylindrical cells, 46 millimetres wide and 120 tall, from plants in Jiangsu and Hebei, with a stated yield of 95%. The iX5 is the first car to use them. The cells are imported from China because AESC paused its South Carolina cell plant in 2025.
For battery and pack engineers, BMW's move puts the 46-series format into high-volume premium cars, and the supply route shows how tariffs and local-content rules still shape sourcing.

stories.headline: Ford's Michigan plant ships its first LFP cells for test fitting in Fathom prototypes
stories.why: Ford's cheaper EV platform depends on these CATL-licensed cells, a test case for Western-built LFP.
body: The first prismatic lithium iron phosphate cells have come off the line at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, marking the end of the pilot phase. The technology is licensed from CATL. The cells go first to Louisville, Kentucky, for fitting in prototypes of the Fathom, the first vehicle on Ford's Universal EV Platform, which enters production in 2027 at a base price of 28,350 dollars.

The plant has been scaled back from 35 to 20 gigawatt-hours a year and from 2,500 to about 1,700 jobs. Ford says the platform has about 20% fewer parts and 25% fewer connecting elements than its current EVs. Range and charging figures have not been published, and no European launch has been confirmed.
For European OEMs weighing their own LFP supply, Ford's licensing route is the model to watch: local production of Chinese chemistry with the original supplier's know-how.

stories.headline: Sany targets Europe's electric truck market with 500 km range and prices 20% below local makers
stories.why: Chinese heavy trucks are coming for the construction and depot segments where Volvo, Scania and Daimler earn good margins.
body: In an interview at IAA Transportation, Sany eTrucks Europe set out its plans. Its flagship e263 tractor has a 620 kWh usable battery and about 500 km of range. The first trucks have been with customers since May 2026, starting with construction uses such as tippers and cement mixers before moving into logistics. Lead times are about four months.

Sany says it aims to price about 20% below European makers. Service runs through the Alltrucks network of about 650 workshops and through Putzmeister, the German concrete pump maker Sany owns. Sany sold about 22,000 electric tractor units in China in 2025 but gave no European sales target.
For European truck makers and their suppliers, this adds price pressure in exactly the segments where electric trucks are taking off first: short, predictable routes with depot charging.

stories.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Accounting, with plugins for QuickBooks, Xero and NetSuite
stories.why: OpenAI keeps packaging ChatGPT by job role, with partner plugins and human sign-off as the template for agent features.
body: OpenAI has launched ChatGPT for Accounting, built around a new Accounting plugin for ChatGPT Business and Work plans. It handles invoice processing, bank reconciliation, month-end reports, data entry and audit preparation, and it shows up in a sidebar next to the chat. Final accounting entries need human approval.

Partner plugins connect to Intuit QuickBooks, Xero, Oracle NetSuite, BILL, FreshBooks, Rillet and Campfire. FourWeekMBA counts eight partner tiles on the launch page, against 33 for ChatGPT for Sales earlier in the week, and notes that the customer results shown are testimonials, not measured outcomes. No pricing was given.

For product teams, the pattern is clear: a general assistant, a role-specific plugin, write access to the system of record, and an approval step before anything final. That approval step is the design choice to copy for any agent that touches money or regulated data.

stories.headline: Swedish physics-simulation firm Algoryx gets Wallenberg Investments as a strategic owner
stories.why: A Swedish simulation specialist is getting long-term backing to build 'physical AI' for heavy machines and robots.
body: Algoryx, a physics-simulation company spun out of Umeå University in 2007, said Wallenberg Investments has become a strategic minority shareholder. The amount was not disclosed. The founders and staff keep the majority. Customers include machine makers, robotics firms, industrial companies and space projects.

The company wants to lead in what it calls physical AI for heavy equipment and mobile robots: simulation detailed and fast enough to train and test machine control in virtual environments before it runs on real hardware. The money will go to hiring, computing capacity and its next product platform, and more fundraising is planned.

For virtual validation teams, Algoryx is a useful reminder that simulation-based training and testing is not only a CAE-vendor topic. Real-time multibody and contact simulation is becoming core tooling for autonomy and off-highway machinery, and Sweden has a notable player in it.

stories.headline: Siemens ends forced project upgrades in TIA Portal V21.1 and links it to its AI engineering agent
stories.why: Automation engineers get continuous software updates without re-validating projects, plus a route to AI-assisted PLC work.
body: Siemens launched TIA Portal V21.1, its automation engineering software, and changed how it is sold and updated. Installed software is now separate from licensing across STEP 7, WinCC Unified and Startdrive, so customers buy features rather than versions. Within V21, users get the latest software without migrating and re-validating their projects.

The release adds multicore programming for S7-1500 controllers and a link to the Eigen Engineering Agent, the AI agent Siemens first showed at Hannover Messe in April. Download is due at the end of November, with delivery in December.

For plants that run test rigs and production lines on Siemens controllers, avoiding re-validation after every upgrade saves real effort. The AI agent link means AI-generated PLC code is arriving in a mainstream engineering tool, so review and sign-off rules for that code are worth settling now.

stories.headline: Deutsche Telekom's Industrial AI Cloud will train microagi's robot skills from simulated factory work
stories.why: Sim-to-real robot training on sovereign German infrastructure targets European manufacturers wary of sending production data abroad.
body: Munich robotics AI company microagi will train its industrial robot models on Deutsche Telekom's Industrial AI Cloud, run by T-Systems at its Munich AI factory. Videos of real workflows are turned into simulations where robots practise tasks, and the learned skill is then moved to the physical robot. The first targets are manufacturing and logistics.
Telekom stresses that production data stays in Germany under the customer's control. No financial terms were disclosed.

For manufacturing and test engineers, this is another sign that simulation is becoming the training ground for factory automation, not only for product design. Data sovereignty is being used as a selling point against US cloud providers. The open question is how well skills learned in simulation hold up on real lines, where parts, lighting and tolerances vary more than in a virtual cell.

stories.headline: Analysts weigh Schaeffler's China exposure and SKF's value ahead of the Vertevo listing
stories.why: The two European bearing majors face different tests: China car demand for Schaeffler, and the automotive spin-off for SKF.
body: UBS kept Schaeffler at Neutral with a price target of 8.10 euros. Analyst David Lesne pointed to China, where car retail sales fell about 25% year on year in the first half of November, with wholesale volumes down almost as much and no sign of recovery. For a supplier with large Chinese automotive volumes, that weakness weighs on bearing and drivetrain orders.

Pareto kept its Buy rating on SKF with a target of 315 kronor ahead of the Vertevo listing on 1 December. It values SKF and Vertevo together at about 320 kronor per SKF share, with Vertevo worth about 8 billion kronor. Pareto expects Vertevo's margin to be about 6% in 2028, with 1.5 billion kronor of investment in 2027 and about 500 million kronor a year of restructuring costs from 2027 to 2029.
For engineers at OEMs and suppliers, Vertevo's restructuring plan and Schaeffler's China exposure will both shape how hard these companies push on price and capacity in the next sourcing rounds.

stories.headline: Two bearing-diagnosis papers fuse motor current with vibration and adapt to new operating conditions
stories.why: Both target a real problem in EV drives: diagnosing bearings that run across many speeds and loads, with sensors already in the motor.
body: A peer-reviewed paper in Processes from Xinjiang University combines vibration and motor-current signals in a two-branch neural network, then links the predicted fault to a knowledge graph of causes and maintenance actions. On a public bearing dataset it reports 98.4% overall accuracy and 100% recognition of combined inner and outer ring faults. Fusing both signals beat either one alone.

A second peer-reviewed paper, in Machines from Anhui University of Science and Technology, tackles the change in operating conditions. It mixes wavelet-based deep features with seven classic statistics and adjusts the model so a diagnoser trained at one speed and load still works at another, using only confident predictions on the new data. It reports average accuracies of 98.7% and 99.5% across six transfer tasks on the Paderborn and HUST datasets.

Both were tested only on lab benchmark data, so these are incremental steps, not field-proven tools. Still, current-based sensing suits EV motors, where current is already measured, and the knowledge-graph step moves toward diagnosis that explains itself to maintenance staff.
